rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The record of what people send ahead and leave behind includes both afterlife deeds and worldly acts or acts done for those who come after them.
rows.anchor: both these types of deeds are being noted by God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imām means leader, guide, and fountainhead; by extension it names a Book that guides and serves as a source, as with the Torah.
rows.anchor: The actual meaning of the word امَمِإِ is “leader, guide and fountainhead.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here imām is the central register recording everyone's deeds for reward or punishment, further affirming that no word or deed escapes God's record.
rows.anchor: it refers to the central register which records the deeds of all people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The city account warns Quraysh that rejecting God's messengers leads to destruction: the first two are rejected, a third supports them, and the people dismiss signs, blame bad luck, and threaten the messengers.
rows.anchor: The Almighty sent two of His messengers to warn the inhabitants of this city; however, they denied both of them.

rows.speaker: exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes identify the unnamed city as Antioch and its messengers as envoys selected from Jesus's disciples, rather than messengers sent by God.
rows.anchor: Our exegetes are of the opinion that the reference is to Antioch and the messengers mentioned here are not the messengers of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers' manner of introduction and their claim under oath show that they are God's envoys, not emissaries of Jesus; their audience's objection to their humanity fits a claim to divine prophethood.
rows.anchor: they are not envoys of Jesus (sws); rather they are envoys of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A destruction of Antioch during Jesus's time would appear in the Gospels and Bible histories, but those sources omit it and historical accounts instead say Antioch led in accepting Jesus.
rows.anchor: neither the Gospels nor Bible history mention it. In fact, history bears witness to the contrary;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article in al-qarya marks the city as already known to the audience.
rows.anchor: the word is defined by the definite article ال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the account is meant to warn Quraysh, its city must be a familiar, famous historical example rather than an unknown event.
rows.anchor: because the purpose of narrating it is to warn the Quraysh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus's mission was to Israel, not the surrounding nations.
rows.anchor: Jesus (sws) was a messenger sent to the Israelites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus stopped his disciples from carrying his message to other nations, undercutting the Antioch identification.
rows.anchor: He in fact stopped his disciples from going to other nations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi calls the Antioch view baseless and introduces several reasons against it.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, this view is baseless because of a number of reasons.

none: Qur'anic text and its English translation only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “to them” refers to the Quraysh.
rows.anchor: The antecedent of the pronoun in مُهَل is the Quraysh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article signals that the audience already knows the city; later indications identify it as Egypt, whose story Quraysh knew well.
rows.anchor: shows that the addressees were aware of it in their minds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words about the messengers coming focus the audience on the circumstances of their mission; recounting the city's story warns Quraysh they will meet the same fate if they follow its people.
rows.anchor: The verse states that the Prophet (sws) should recount the anecdote of the people of the city before his addressees

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 14 explains the sending mentioned in verse 13: two messengers came first, were rejected, and then received God's help through a third, after which they called people to obey their message.
rows.anchor: The Almighty initially sent two messengers to them but they rejected these messengers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two are Moses and Aaron; Islahi says this is the sole instance in prophetic history of two messengers being sent simultaneously to one people, an arrangement discussed in earlier sūrahs.
rows.anchor: there is only once instance when two messengers were simultaneously sent by God to a people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the Qur’an introduces the third helper at verse 20 and records his memorable speech in support of Moses.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān has introduced him in verse 20 ahead

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though no messenger in the technical sense, the believer courageously defended the messengers; Islahi compares his standing among Moses's followers to Abū Bakr's among Muhammad's.
rows.anchor: Though he was not a messenger in the technical sense, yet he undertook a fearless effort to defend and support the messengers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The identical introduction in 36:20 and 28:20 identifies the believer as the man who warned Moses of a death plot after the Egyptian killing, prompting Moses to flee to Midian.
rows.anchor: In precisely the same words, he is introduced in Sūrah Qas@as@:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer belonged to Pharaoh's royal family, advocated truth, and sympathized with Moses even before Moses received prophethood.
rows.anchor: It is evident from verse 40 of Sūrah Mu’min that he belonged to the royal family and was a great advocate of the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Pharaoh and his courtiers decided to kill Moses, the believer spoke in Pharaoh's court; Islahi cites that speech from verses 26–45 of Sūrah Mu’min as evidence of his status and support.
rows.anchor: This speech is cited by the Qur’ān in Sūrah Mu’min.

rows.speaker: Pharaoh
rows.claim: Pharaoh proposes killing Moses, claiming fear that Moses will change their religion and spread disorder, and daring him to call on his Lord for aid.
rows.anchor: The Pharaoh said to his courtiers: “Let me slay Moses; if he is truthful let him call his Lord.

rows.speaker: Moses
rows.claim: Moses seeks God's protection from every arrogant person who rejects the Day of Reckoning.
rows.anchor: Moses said: “I take refuge with my Lord and your Lord from the evil of every arrogant person

rows.speaker: a believer from the Pharaoh’s family
rows.claim: The hidden believer objects to killing a man who worships God and brings clear signs: if Moses is false, harm is his; if true, some threatened punishment will reach them, and God does not vindicate a blatant liar or transgressor.
rows.anchor: But a believer from the Pharaoh’s family who had till then hidden his faith, said: “Would you slay a man merely because he says:

rows.speaker: a believer from the Pharaoh’s family
rows.claim: The believer warns that present dominance cannot save them from God's torment and that God does not approve of servants being oppressed.
rows.anchor: a believer from the Pharaoh’s family who had till then hidden his faith, said:

rows.speaker: Pharaoh
rows.claim: Pharaoh counters that his considered opinion is sound and that he is guiding the people on the straight path.
rows.anchor: The Pharaoh said: “I am giving my calculated opinion and remember that I am guiding you towards exactly the straight path.

rows.speaker: a believer from the Pharaoh’s family
rows.claim: The believer warns of the punishments that overtook Noah's people, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and later nations; he fears the coming Day of flight with no rescuer, recalls Egypt's doubts after Joseph's clear signs, and warns that one whom God misguides has no guide.
rows.anchor: And he who had embraced faith said: “O People of My Nation! I fear the same punishment will befall you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi explains that those who overstep bounds and dispute revelations without proof are hated by God and believers, and that God seals every arrogant tyrant's heart.
rows.anchor: In this manner does God lead astray those who exceed bounds and are afflicted with doubts

rows.speaker: Pharaoh
rows.claim: Pharaoh orders Hāmān to build a tower from which he can inspect the heavens for Moses's Lord, whom he declares a liar.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh said: “O Hāmān! Build me a tower that I may peep in the edges of the heavens
